name: Permissions Policy and iframe allow
plain: HTTP header and iframe allow attribute that decide which features a page or frame may use.
meaning: Lets a site disable features for itself and its iframes. MDN lists 51 directives; each can be self, a list of origins, or none. A feature blocked here never reaches the user prompt.

access.prompt_ui: Server sent header plus iframe allow attribute; cross-origin frames get a feature only if both parent and frame allow it.
steps: Feature granted to frame or blocked

limits.headline: Can turn features off for itself and its embedded frames
limits.user_action: Nothing. The site sets rules in its headers or in an iframe
can: Block features like camera, location, or microphone for itself
Allow a feature in an iframe only if both sides agree
Stop embedded ads or widgets from using sensors
Set 51 or so rules, each for self, listed sites, or none
cannot: Give itself more than you allow in the browser
Turn on a feature you blocked
Let an embedded frame use a feature the parent blocked
Skip your pop up for a feature

story.what_it_is: A site rule that says which features the page and its embedded frames are allowed to use.

marketing.name: Permissions Policy
marketing.pitch: Docs explain it as a header that lets sites turn browser features on or off for themselves and embeds.

marketing.name: Permissions Policy
marketing.pitch: Chrome documents how to control feature access for your page and third party frames.

story.for_you: You never see it. Its job is to protect you: a site can promise that an embedded ad or video cannot reach your camera or location. If a site forgets, an embed might not work.
story.for_makers: Sites use it to lock off powerful features from third party frames, such as ads or widgets. It lowers the damage if an embed is hacked. Embedding services must also ask for the access they need through the allow attribute.

use_cases.example: A site embeds a video meeting in a frame and allows camera and microphone only for that frame.
A publisher blocks geolocation and camera for all ad frames so ads cannot reach them.
A game portal allows fullscreen and gamepad access only to the game frame.
A shop allows the payment request feature only for its payment provider frame.
A bank turns off camera, microphone and location for its own pages.
A team tests that a third party widget breaks cleanly when a feature is blocked.
A company web portal blocks sensors for all embedded dashboards.

risks: Only as safe as the site makes it

technical_bounds: Camera, microphone, geolocation default to self
Cannot grant what the user denied
